# The Edinburgh festival season

Everything else happening in Edinburgh alongside the Fringe — the other August
festivals, the rest of the summer, and the seasonal things that are not
festivals at all. Compiled once, refined in place.

This page exists because the product's premise ("4,206 shows is too many") is
only true of one festival. In August the city runs at least eight programmes
concurrently, and they are not variations on the Fringe: they differ in scale by
two orders of magnitude, in how an event behaves in time, in whether a ticket
exists, and in whether the data is reachable at all.

## Key insights

- August is at least eight overlapping festivals, not one — the Fringe is ~80% of the events and all of the noise.
- One free API already carries all 11 festivals, with coordinates, start times, durations and prices.
- That API has no sold-out field — our sharpest live signal does not survive a move off the Fringe scraper.
- Its licence bars redistributing dumps to third parties, and we commit our data to a public repo.
- "An event" is six different shapes: daily run, short season, one-off, nightly anchor, drop-in, all-day occasion.
- The Art Festival is 40+ mostly-free drop-in exhibitions with no start time — a shape nothing in the product models.
- Summer starts in June: Hidden Door, the Meadows, the Carnival and Jazz & Blues all finish before the Fringe opens.

## The August cluster (2026)

Eight programmes overlap almost completely. Every one of them is running on
15–19 August; a visitor in the city that week is inside all of them at once
whether they know it or not.

| Festival | Dates | Scale | Where |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Festival Fringe** | 7–31 Aug | 4,232 shows / 61,277 performances / 306 venues / 77 countries | citywide |
| **International Festival (EIF)** | 7–30 Aug | 147 performances / 44 countries / 2 exhibitions | a few large halls |
| **Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo** | 7–29 Aug (not Sundays) | one show, ~800 performers, ~9,000 seats a night, ~230,000 a year | one venue |
| **Edinburgh Deaf Festival** | 7–16 Aug | 80+ events | Deaf Action + Fringe venues |
| **International Film Festival (EIFF)** | 13–19 Aug | 38 new features, 21 world premieres | 5–6 cinemas + pop-up |
| **Art Festival** | 14–30 Aug | 40+ exhibitions, 25+ partner galleries, mostly free | galleries citywide |
| **International Book Festival** | 15–30 Aug | ~600 events / ~600 writers / 41 countries | one campus, 3 rooms |
| **Fringe by the Sea** | 31 Jul–9 Aug | a small Fringe of its own | **North Berwick, not Edinburgh** |

Two things fall out of the table:

- **Volume is overwhelmingly Fringe.** Every non-Fringe August festival added
  together is roughly 900 events against the Fringe's 4,232 shows — the Fringe is
  ~82% of the cluster. (Corrected 2026-08-09: this read 3,649, the 4 June
  programme-launch figure, which was ~15% short of the delivered festival; the
  conclusion is unchanged and slightly stronger. Updated 2026-09-11 from the
  opening-day 4,206 to the festival's final closing count, 4,232 — the ~82%
  share is unchanged. See
  [edinburgh-market-and-audience/](../edinburgh-market-and-audience/README.md) for both corrections.)
  Any ranking that sorts purely on relevance or proximity will show a Fringe-only
  city.
- **Scarcity runs the other way.** A Fringe show typically plays ~25 times. A
  Book Festival author appears once. An EIFF screening is often a single
  showing. The events that are hardest to replace are the ones the volume
  ranking buries.

**Free Fringe (4–30 Aug) and Free Festival (6–30 Aug)** are not separate
festivals for data purposes — they are producers whose shows appear inside the
Fringe programme, so the existing catalogue already contains them.

**Edinburgh Summer Sessions** (24–29 Aug per a listings aggregator, not yet
confirmed against a promoter source) is an outdoor concert series rather than a
festival programme, and is listed here only so a later pass knows it was
considered.

## The rest of the summer

The season starts in June and the pre-August festivals are almost entirely free
and outdoor — a materially different offer from the ticketed August cluster.

| Event | Dates (2026) | Shape |
|---|---|---|
| **Hidden Door** | 3–7 Jun | pop-up arts festival, The Paper Factory |
| **Meadows Festival** | 6–7 Jun | free community weekend, one park |
| **International Children's Festival (Imaginate)** | May–Jun | children's theatre |
| **Jazz & Blues Festival** | 17–26 Jul | 100–170+ concerts (sources differ), clubs to concert halls |
| **Edinburgh Festival Carnival / Multicultural Festival** | 19 Jul | one-day city-centre parade |
| **Folk & Food Festival** | 24 Jul–2 Aug | free-entry food and folk, George Square Gardens |

Outside the summer entirely, and named only so they are not re-researched:
Science Festival (April), Beltane Fire Festival (30 April), Storytelling
Festival (October), Hogmanay (December).

## The seasonal city that is not a festival

The brief's user — someone with a free hour — is not only choosing between
shows. Guide coverage of an Edinburgh summer converges on the same non-ticketed
list: Arthur's Seat and Holyrood Park, the Royal Botanic Garden, Inverleith
Park, the Meadows, Princes Street Gardens, Portobello beach (swimming), the
Water of Leith walkway, and the Saturday markets (Stockbridge, Grassmarket,
Castle Terrace).

Two honest caveats:

- **This is guide-site material, not a dataset.** There is no listings feed for
  "the Meadows is nice in August." Anything the product does here is a
  hand-curated short list, and should be sized accordingly. (Softened
  2026-09-01: for *attractions* specifically, OSM + Wikidata are a free
  machine-readable base layer, and the wider source landscape — for
  Edinburgh and every other festival city — now has its own page,
  [city-context-sources/](../city-context-sources/README.md). The claim
  stands for the curated "nice in August" judgment itself.)
- **The repo already has the seam.** `js/places.js` geocodes arbitrary
  non-show destinations through Nominatim, so a curated seasonal place is
  representable today without new infrastructure.

## What "an event" means differs per festival

This is the finding that matters most for design, and it is not a branding
question. Across the eight August programmes an event behaves in one of six
ways in time, and the differences change what the product can truthfully
promise:

1. **Run** — repeats near-daily at one time across a long run (Fringe, Fringe by
   the Sea). Missing it today costs nothing.
2. **Short season** — a handful of dated performances, often at differing times
   (EIF theatre/opera/dance, larger Deaf Festival work). Each date is scarce.
3. **One-off** — happens exactly once (Book Festival author events, most EIFF
   screenings, Jazz concerts, talks). Missing it is terminal.
4. **Nightly anchor** — the same show every night, one venue, huge capacity,
   sold months ahead (the Tattoo). Behaves like a fixed commitment, not a
   candidate.
5. **Drop-in** — no start time at all: opening hours and a duration the visitor
   chooses (Art Festival exhibitions, typically ~10:00–17:00, mostly free).
6. **All-day occasion** — a single dated outdoor thing with no seat and no slot
   (the Carnival parade, Meadows Festival, Folk & Food).

Only shape 1 is modelled today. Shapes 3 and 5 are the ones that break existing
assumptions hardest: a one-off is a point rather than a lane, and a drop-in has
no start time to reach in time for.

## Locations

- **The Fringe is citywide** (306 venues); everything else is concentrated.
- **The Book Festival is effectively one campus** — Edinburgh Futures Institute
  (1 Lauriston Place), plus McEwan Hall and, new for 2026, Greyfriars Kirk. All
  within a few minutes' walk of each other and of the Fringe's Bristo Square
  cluster.
- **EIF uses a handful of large halls** — Usher Hall, Festival Theatre, The
  Queen's Hall, Church Hill Theatre. Church Hill is the outlier, ~25 minutes
  south of the centre on foot.
- **EIFF spreads deliberately** — Cineworld Fountainbridge, Filmhouse, Cameo,
  Monkey Barrel, plus **Leith Theatre** (a genuine 30+ minute walk from the Old
  Town) and a pop-up screen at the National Gallery.
- **The Tattoo is the Castle Esplanade**, which also means the top of the Royal
  Mile is congested nightly.
- **Fringe by the Sea is in North Berwick**, ~25 miles east — a train journey,
  not a walk. Any travel estimate that treats it as a city venue is wrong by an
  order of magnitude.

## Can we actually get the data?

Yes, and better than expected — with two sharp edges.

### The Edinburgh Festivals Listings API

`api.edinburghfestivalcity.com`, run by Festivals Edinburgh Limited, originally
built by the Science Festival in 2016. It is the **official** listings database
for all 11 major festivals and is **free to use** with a registered access key.

- **Coverage.** The `festival` parameter accepts `fringe, demofringe, jazz,
  book, international, tattoo, art, hogmanay, science, imaginate, film, mela,
  storytelling`. The status page confirms 2026 data is loaded for the
  Children's, Science, Tattoo, Film, International, Jazz, Fringe, Art and Book
  festivals.
- **Fields we need are present.** Events carry `festival`, `title`, `genre`,
  `genre_tags`, `artist`, `country`, `description`, images, a venue record with
  `latitude`/`longitude`, wheelchair access, and a `performances[]` array of
  `{start, end, duration_minutes, price, concession, price_string,
  is_at_fixed_time}`. Query parameters include lat/lon/distance, date range,
  price range, genre, venue and `modified_from` for incremental sync.
- **`is_at_fixed_time` is the drop-in flag** — the API already distinguishes a
  timed performance from an open-hours one, which is exactly the shape
  distinction the product needs.
- **It carries real prices.** The edfringe GraphQL API deliberately does not
  (only `priceType` flags); the Listings API returns `price` and `price_string`.
  This would close a limitation the product brief currently apologises for.

**Edge 1 — no availability.** The performance object has no sold-out, on-sale or
remaining-tickets field. The Fringe scraper's `ticketStatus` has no counterpart
here, so for non-Fringe festivals the product cannot honestly say whether a
ticket exists. Anything that implies parity would be inventing data.

**Edge 2 — the licence bars redistributing dumps.** Commercial use is explicitly
permitted and attribution is required (a visible credit plus a link to the API).
But developer users "must not redistribute listings to third parties by means of
either data feeds or data dumps", and applications must refresh at least every
24 hours. This repo currently **commits its normalized catalogue to a public git
repo and serves it as a static JSON file from GitHub Pages** — a pattern that
needs an explicit answer from Festivals Edinburgh before it is used with their
data. It is the one genuine blocker found.

**Edge 3 — Fringe data specifically is approval-gated and link-restricted**
(found 2026-07-31 in the ticketing pass): developers build against a randomised
`demofringe` dataset and must [submit the app for review](https://api.edinburghfestivalcity.com/documentation/fringe_approval)
before live Fringe access; the Fringe terms require that show links go **only to
edfringe.com** — "not… any other ticketing site, including the venue's own
site". Sync is near-real-time (`modified_from`, "a delay of a few minutes"), and
a beta [MCP endpoint](https://api.edinburghfestivalcity.com/documentation/mcp)
exists. The full ticketing/provider picture is on
[edinburgh-fringe-ticketing/](../edinburgh-fringe-ticketing/README.md).

### Keeping the Fringe on its own source

The existing edfringe GraphQL scraper stays the better Fringe source: it carries
per-performance `ticketStatus`, the 104-label subgenre taxonomy, content
warnings and age guidance the Listings API does not expose at the same fidelity.
The realistic architecture is two adapters into one normalized schema, not a
migration.

### Other aggregators

**Data Thistle** (`edinburghfestival.datathistle.com`) publishes combined
listings across the Fringe, International, Book, Jazz, Tattoo, Art, Film, Free
Fringe, Free Festival and Fringe by the Sea, and sells an events API — evidence
that cross-festival listings are a real product, and the closest thing found to
a direct multi-festival competitor.

The Listings API's own project gallery lists 13 apps built on it (Plan My
Fringe, FringeFlow, TicketBadger, Frindr, myFestival, Festival Clock, Fringe
Vibes and others). Notably, nearly all of them are named and framed around the
**Fringe** despite the API carrying all 11 festivals — no listed project claims
cross-festival planning as its point. That gap is unverified beyond the gallery
blurbs and belongs in the competitor page once someone actually uses them.

## Sources

- [#MixItUp at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe and discover your new favourite show (edfringe.com, 7 August 2026)](https://www.edfringe.com/about-us/news-and-blog/mixitup-at-the-edinburgh-festival-fringe-and-discover-your-new-favourite-show/) — the Fringe's opening-day 2026 scale: 4,206 shows, 299 venues, 74 countries, 60,000+ performances.
- [Edinburgh Festival Fringe 2026 concludes with its 80th anniversary firmly in sight (edfringe.com, 31 August 2026)](https://www.edfringe.com/about-us/news-and-blog/edinburgh-festival-fringe-2026-concludes-with-its-80th-anniversary-firmly-in-sight/) — the Fringe's final delivered 2026 scale: 4,232 shows, 306 venues, 77 countries, 61,277 performances, used in the table above.
- [Edinburgh Festivals: What's On in 2026 (Edinburgh Festival City)](https://www.edinburghfestivalcity.com/inspiration/573-edinburgh-festivals-whats-on-in-2026)

## Open questions

- **Does the licence permit our static-file architecture?** The one blocker.
  Committing Listings API data to a public repo and serving it as a JSON file
  from GitHub Pages may read as redistributing a data dump. Needs a direct
  answer from Festivals Edinburgh, not an inference from the terms page.
- **What does the API actually return?** Every field claim here comes from the
  documentation, not from an authenticated response — nobody has registered a
  key. (Narrowed 2026-07-31: the public explorer confirms 2026 Fringe data is
  loaded, and the per-performance field list was verified against the events
  documentation; per-festival event counts and `is_at_fixed_time` population
  remain unchecked.)
- **Is `is_at_fixed_time` enough to derive event shape?** It separates timed from
  drop-in, but not one-off from run from nightly. Those may be derivable by
  counting performances per event — unconfirmed.
- **Does the API carry the Deaf Festival?** It is not in the `festival`
  parameter list, and its events are produced with the Fringe — so they may
  appear under `fringe` with no distinguishing marker, which would make the
  festival invisible in a festival filter.
- **Jazz & Blues event count.** Sources say "over 170 performances", "more than
  100 concerts" and "over 150 concerts" — no authoritative figure found.
- **Cross-festival audience behaviour.** Still no *current*, Fringe-specific
  data on how many Fringe-goers attend a second festival, or whether the two
  are the same crowd — [edinburgh-market-and-audience/](../edinburgh-market-and-audience/README.md)
  worked this open question 2026-08-16 and found only a 15-year-old,
  unverifiable lead plus a forthcoming 2026 study worth watching; see that
  page rather than duplicating the finding here. The whole "help people see
  the diversity of Edinburgh" goal still rests on an unmeasured assumption
  that they would attend a second festival if they knew.
- **Non-festival seasonal has no source of truth.** If a curated places list
  ships, who maintains it and how does it stay true?
- **Is a multi-festival product still called EdFringeNow?** A naming/brand
  question for a human, raised here only because the research makes it real.

## Growth log

- **2026-07-31** — page created. Seeded from research into the other Edinburgh

  six event *shapes* that distinguish a Fringe run from a one-off screening, a

  coordinates, times, durations and real prices, its missing availability field,
  and its no-redistribution licence term that conflicts with this repo's

  `modified_from` sync and the beta MCP endpoint, and narrowed the "what does
  the API actually return" open question (2026 Fringe data confirmed loaded via
  the public explorer; still no authenticated call). Cross-linked the new
  edinburgh-fringe-ticketing page.
- **2026-08-09** — corrected the Fringe's row in the August cluster table and the
  volume arithmetic beneath it from the 4 June programme-launch snapshot (3,649
  shows / 53,884 performances / 258 venues / 71 countries) to the Fringe
  Society's opening-day figures (4,206 / 60,000+ / 299 / 74). The superseded
  numbers and the reason they were wrong are kept on
  [edinburgh-market-and-audience/](../edinburgh-market-and-audience/README.md), which owns them. The
  Fringe's share of the cluster moves from ~80% to ~82%, so the page's
  conclusions and its Key insights header are unchanged — only the figures moved.
- **2026-08-16** — narrowed the cross-festival-audience open question to point
  at [edinburgh-market-and-audience/](../edinburgh-market-and-audience/README.md), which worked it
  this pass in full (a forthcoming 2026 Fringe-specific impact study, and why
  the one cross-festival figure found is not trustworthy enough to cite as
  fact) rather than duplicate the finding on both pages. No claim on this page
  itself changed; header unchanged.
- **2026-09-01** — softened the "no listings feed" caveat under *The seasonal
  city that is not a festival*: the new
  [city-context-sources/](../city-context-sources/README.md) page now owns
  the machine-readable source landscape for non-festival events and

1	# Edinburgh Fringe ticketing & providers
2	
3	Who actually sells an Edinburgh Fringe ticket, who all the venue operators
4	("providers") are, whether a third party can sell tickets itself, and whether
5	any provider or aggregator feed could replace scraping edfringe.com. Compiled
6	once, refined in place.
7	
8	This page exists to answer a specific owner question — *"are edfringe.com and
9	edfest.com both just fronts for the event organizers?"* — and the answer turned
10	out to be half yes: one of the two is exactly that, and it is not the one the
11	product depends on.
12	
13	## Key insights
14	
15	- edfringe.com is an independent charity's box office, not the venues' — the venues' own storefront is edfest.com.
16	- Every ticketed show must give the Fringe box office at least 25% of its tickets; venues sell the rest themselves.
17	- One vendor, Red61, powers ten of the fifteen biggest operators' box offices. Provider access is one Red61 question.
18	- Nobody offers an affiliate or agent scheme — not the Society, not the venues. Deep links earn nothing, anywhere.
19	- Our own scrape is the provider census: 24 operator families cover 83% of the programme; the tail is 171 small venues.
20	- The official Listings API bans linking to any ticket seller except edfringe.com — even the venue's own site.
21	- Only the edfringe GraphQL has availability for the whole programme. The scrape cannot be retired.
22	
23	## Who actually sells a Fringe ticket
24	
25	The premise to correct first: **edfringe.com is not a front for the venue
26	operators.** It is run by the [Edinburgh Festival Fringe Society](https://www.oscr.org.uk/about-charities/search-the-register/charity-details?number=SC002995),
27	an independent registered Scottish charity (SC002995, income £8.28m FY2024)
28	governed by an open **£5/year membership** that elects its board — structurally
29	separate from the operators, and [publicly feuded with](https://www.scotsman.com/whats-on/arts-and-entertainment/edinburgh-festival-fringe-longest-running-venue-operator-says-he-has-lost-confidence-in-the-fringe-society-3791322)
30	by them at times. The Society performs no curation (open access: anyone with a
31	show, a willing venue and the registration fee is in the programme) and runs the
32	central box office.
33	
34	**The allocation model** is the load-bearing mechanic, from the Society's own
35	[participant guidance](https://help.registration.edfringe.com/create-or-edit-a-show/payout-and-fringe-allocation.aspx):
36	every ticketed show must allocate a **minimum 25% of tickets per performance**
37	to the Fringe Box Office (sliding scale above that), on which the Society takes
38	**5%+VAT commission**; the venue sells the remainder through its own box office
39	at its own rate ([Assembly charges 4%+VAT](https://s3.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com/cdn.assemblyfestival.com/Assembly%20Festival%202026%20Information%20Pack%20for%20Performers%20(6).pdf);
40	[Summerhall 8%](https://www.summerhallarts.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/Summerhall-Arts-Festival-Information-Pack_2025_web.pdf),
41	and reports that ~70% of its tickets nonetheless sell through the Fringe box
42	office). This model is why the scrape's `NO_ALLOCATION_CONTACT_VENUE` status
43	exists: when the Society's allocation for a performance is exhausted, [the
44	official advice](https://www.edfringe.com/faqs/) is to check with the venue box
45	office — the ticket may still exist, just not in the channel we can see. In the
46	2026 data that status marks 1,279 of ~59,900 performances (2.1%), concentrated
47	at the big operators.
48	
49	**Platforms:** since March 2025 edfringe.com runs on an interim site built by
50	Australian agency equ on its Tikketr platform (the GraphQL the scraper hits;
51	the [official app](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.tikketr.edfringe.prod&hl=en)
52	is `com.tikketr.edfringe.prod` and takes [~30% of all ticket sales](https://www.edfringe.com/about-us/news-and-blog/our-digital-transformation-strategy-march-2025/)).
53	[Red61 ran the Society box office 2009–2023](https://www.red61.com/news/red61-celebrates-20-years-at-the-edinburgh-festival-fringe/)
54	and still powers the venue side (17 federated VIA instances in 2024). A
55	permanent replacement site is being [built by Storm ID for Fringe 2027](https://www.edfringe.com/about-us/news-and-blog/fringe-society-appoints-storm-id-to-develop-new-website-for-the-fringe/) —
56	meaning **the scraper's target platform is explicitly interim**.
57	
58	## edfest.com — the venues' own storefront
59	
60	The other half of the owner's premise is correct. [edfest.com](https://edfest.com/about)
61	is operated by **Showcatcher Ltd** ([company 07628569](https://find-and-update.company-information.service.gov.uk/company/07628569/officers),
62	lead director William Burdett-Coutts — Assembly's founder and artistic
63	director): a cross-venue storefront formed by the major operators — Assembly,
64	C ARTS, Gilded Balloon, Just the Tonic, Pleasance, Underbelly, ZOO (Summerhall
65	was an eighth founder and has left the list). It explicitly
66	[acts "as an agent on behalf of multiple venues and producers"](https://edfest.com/faqs)
67	on Red61 rails, sells only participating venues' shows in one basket, caps
68	booking fees at £5, and fronts the [Love the Fringe membership](https://theqr.co.uk/2026/06/04/edfest-2026-launch-fringe-crisis-how-to-save-on-tickets/).
69	So the accurate map: **edfringe.com = the charity's central box office;
70	edfest.com = the big operators' joint venture; venue sites = each operator's
71	own channel** — three parallel channels selling overlapping inventory.
72	
73	(Also answered: **Edinburgh Playhouse** is an [ATG receiving house](https://www.atgtickets.com/venues/edinburgh-playhouse/),
74	not a Fringe operator — but it *is* [registered Fringe venue 59](https://www.edfringe.com/tickets/venues/edinburgh-playhouse)
75	in 2026, hosting four big ATG-ticketed comedy one-nighters.)
76	
77	## The provider census
78	
79	The completeness question has a clean answer: the Fringe is open-access but
80	**being "in the Fringe" requires paid registration with the Society**, and
81	venue registration (free) puts every venue in the
82	[public directory](https://tickets.edfringe.com/venues) — so the registered
83	catalogue we already scrape **is by construction the exhaustive universe** of
84	providers. Our `data/venues.json` carries 301 registered venue records for
85	2026; grouping the 294 venues that carry shows in
86	[`data/normalized/shows.json`](https://github.com/missingbulb/EdFringeNow/blob/main/data/normalized/shows.json)
87	by operator family gives the census (computed 2026-07-31, 4,100 shows):
88	
89	| Operator | Venues | Shows | Own online box office |
90	|---|---:|---:|---|
91	| theSpaceUK | 6 | 483 | Red61 (tickets.thespaceuk.com) |
92	| Laughing Horse Free Festival | 18 | 320 | free; PWYC advance via Fringe box office |
93	| Assembly | 8 | 300 | Red61 (assemblyfestival.com) |
94	| Pleasance | 5 | 271 | Red61 (pleasance.co.uk `/via/tickets/…`) |
95	| Just the Tonic | 7 | 216 | Red61 (edinburgh.justthetonic.com) |
96	| Hoots | 5 | 201 | — |
97	| Greenside | 2 | 200 | none found — effectively edfringe-only |
98	| Gilded Balloon | 4 | 198 | Red61 (tickets.gildedballoon.co.uk) |
99	| Underbelly | 4 | 193 | Red61 (underbellyedinburgh.co.uk) |
100	| PBH's Free Fringe | 25 | 190 | unticketed — bucket donations only |
101	| Monkey Barrel | 5 | 144 | Line-Up for own sales; Fringe runs via edfringe |
102	| C ARTS / C venues | 4 | 111 | Red61 (CtheArts.com) |
103	| The Stand | 6 | 109 | in-house (thestand.co.uk) |
104	| Summerhall | 1 | 82 | Red61 (tickets.summerhallarts.co.uk) |
105	| Paradise Green | 2 | 75 | volunteer-run non-profit |
106	| EIFF (Film Festival screenings) | 6 | 63 | own festival ticketing |
107	| Braw Venues (Hill St, Grand Lodge) | 2 | 58 | — |
108	| ZOO | 2 | 51 | Red61 (tickets.zoofestival.co.uk) |
109	| Royal Scots Club | 3 | 34 | — |
110	| Scottish Storytelling Centre | 1 | 33 | Red61 |
111	| Scottish Comedy Festival | 2 | 26 | — |
112	| Traverse | 3 | 12 | **Spektrix — publicly readable API** |
113	| Bedlam (EUTC) | 1 | 12 | — |
114	| French Institute | 1 | 3 | — |
115	
116	The remaining **171 venues carry 715 shows (17%)** — churches, pubs, one-room
117	independents (largest: Edinburgh New Town Church, 43 shows; The Jazz Bar, 37).
118	The census caveat: grouping is by venue-name matching, so a mis-named venue can
119	mis-file — treat counts as ±small, not gospel.
120	
121	**The one gap in "exhaustive":** [PBH's Free Fringe makes Society registration
122	optional](https://freefringe.org.uk/performers-faq/) ("It's not compulsory to be
123	in the program"). PBH's own site lists roughly 800 entries for 2026; only 183
124	PBH shows are in the edfringe catalogue. Those unregistered shows exist only in
125	PBH's listings and the printed Wee Blue Book — invisible to edfringe, to the
126	official Listings API, and to us. [Laughing Horse requires registration](https://freefestival.co.uk/Perform_with_us.aspx)
127	("All of our shows must be entered into the Official Fringe Programme"), so its
128	320 shows are fully covered. Free shows otherwise appear in the data like any
129	other (399 shows `FREE_NON_TICKETED`, 23 `FREE_TICKETED`).
130	
131	## Can we sell tickets ourselves? No — and nobody can
132	
133	The verified negative, adversarially checked: **no open affiliate, agent,
134	reseller, white-label or purchase-API route into Fringe ticketing exists.**
135	
136	- The **Fringe Society** offers no scheme of any kind; its
137	  [ticketing T&Cs](https://tickets.edfringe.com/terms-and-conditions) bar using
138	  tickets "for any commercial, business or re-sale purposes", and its current
139	  Tikketr platform has no public partner API at all.
140	- **No venue operator** advertises an affiliate or agent programme. The big
141	  operators channelled exactly this energy into their own closed joint venture —
142	  edfest.com — rather than opening a channel to outsiders.
143	- The **platform layer** has the technology but not the access:
144	  [Spektrix runs a dedicated Agency API](https://integrate.spektrix.com/docs/agentguide)
145	  (third-party agents buying on a credit agreement the venue sets up per-agent)
146	  and [Red61 VIA offers APIs, white-label sales and cross-selling](https://www.red61.com/ticketing-solutions/) —
147	  but in every case access is granted per-client under a negotiated commercial
148	  agreement. No self-service signup, no published rates.
149	- Existing "third-party sellers" prove the pattern: See Tickets and Ents24
150	  retail [The Stand's own club shows](https://www.seetickets.com/venue/the-stand-comedy-club/8933)
151	  under explicit venue agency deals; TodayTix and Fever carry **no** actual
152	  Edinburgh Fringe inventory (London transfers and previews only); LivingSocial
153	  retails Love the Fringe *memberships*, not tickets. New for 2026, a
154	  [Sold Out Board lottery pilot](https://www.theticketingbusiness.com/2026/07/west-end-style-lottery-ticketing-system-coming-to-edinburgh-fringe/)
155	  resells last tickets for sold-out shows at face value — also a closed
156	  arrangement.
157	
158	Bottom line for this product: "selling tickets ourselves" would mean separate
159	negotiated agent agreements with dozens of operators across at least five
160	ticketing platforms, with no published programme to even apply to. The realistic
161	ceiling is **deep links to each seller — which earn nothing**, because no
162	commission scheme exists anywhere in the Fringe ecosystem. (This kills the
163	hoped-for ticket-affiliate revenue path; `shared/affiliates.js` stays a
164	travel/accommodation monetisation seam only.)
165	
166	## Can anything replace the edfringe scrape? Mostly no
167	
168	- **The official [Edinburgh Festivals Listings API](https://api.edinburghfestivalcity.com/documentation)**
169	  is the only licensed catalogue alternative: free, official, same registered-show
170	  universe, per-performance start/end/price, a near-real-time
171	  `modified_from` sync ("a delay of a few minutes"), 2026 Fringe data loaded,
172	  and a beta [MCP endpoint](https://api.edinburghfestivalcity.com/documentation/mcp).
173	  But Fringe access is **approval-gated** (build against a randomised
174	  `demofringe` dataset, [submit the app for review](https://api.edinburghfestivalcity.com/documentation/fringe_approval)),
175	  it has **no availability/sold-out field**, and its licence adds a sharp rule:
176	  [links for Fringe shows must go to edfringe.com only](https://api.edinburghfestivalcity.com/documentation/fringe_approval) —
177	  "not… any other ticketing site, including the venue's own site". An
178	  API-approved product could not deep-link to venue box offices.
179	- **Venue operators:** probed directly, the big operators publish nothing
180	  machine-readable (Assembly: locked CMS; Gilded Balloon: WordPress with no
181	  event type; Pleasance/Underbelly/The Stand: server-rendered HTML; Monkey
182	  Barrel: Wix). Two real exceptions, found and verified by live fetch:
183	  **Traverse** exposes a fully public
184	  [Spektrix v3 JSON API](https://system.spektrix.com/traverse/api/v3/events)
185	  including **live per-performance seat availability** (a fetched 2 Aug 2026
186	  performance returned `available: 19, capacity: 302`), and **Summerhall Arts**'
187	  festival site has an open [WordPress REST API with events and performances](https://festival.summerhallarts.co.uk/wp-json/wp/v2/types).
188	  Together they cover ~94 of 4,100 shows — real, but not a strategy.
189	- **Aggregators:** [Data Thistle](https://www.datathistle.com/what-we-do/for-listings-suppliers/)
190	  has genuine full-Fringe coverage but is paid, contact-for-pricing; Skiddle's
191	  API is beta and non-commercial-only with thin coverage; WeGotTickets,
192	  Eventbrite and Ents24 carry effectively nothing.
193	
194	**The verdict:** for the full programme *with availability* — the thing the Now
195	page's honesty depends on — **the edfringe GraphQL scrape has no replacement.**
196	The defensible end-state is: official Listings API as the licensed catalogue
197	backbone *if* its approval and linking rules are acceptable, with a slimmed
198	edfringe probe kept solely as the availability overlay — or simply keep the
199	scrape as-is, knowing its platform is interim (Storm ID site lands for 2027, so
200	the scraper breaks on that timetable regardless).
201	
202	## Sources
203	
204	- [Fringe Society charity record (OSCR SC002995)](https://www.oscr.org.uk/about-charities/search-the-register/charity-details?number=SC002995)
205	- [Edinburgh Festival Fringe Society (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edinburgh_Festival_Fringe_Society)

211	- [Fringe Society appoints Storm ID to develop new website (edfringe.com)](https://www.edfringe.com/about-us/news-and-blog/fringe-society-appoints-storm-id-to-develop-new-website-for-the-fringe/)
212	- [Red61 celebrates 20 years at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe](https://www.red61.com/news/red61-celebrates-20-years-at-the-edinburgh-festival-fringe/)

218	- [Showcatcher Ltd officers (Companies House)](https://find-and-update.company-information.service.gov.uk/company/07628569/officers)

233	- [Edinburgh Festivals Listings API — Fringe approval process](https://api.edinburghfestivalcity.com/documentation/fringe_approval)
234	- [Edinburgh Festivals Listings API — licence](https://api.edinburghfestivalcity.com/licence)
235	- [Edinburgh Festivals Listings API — MCP endpoint (beta)](https://api.edinburghfestivalcity.com/documentation/mcp)

238	- [2026 operator census computed from the repo's scraped catalogue (shows.json)](https://github.com/missingbulb/EdFringeNow/blob/main/data/normalized/shows.json)
239	
240	## Open questions
241	
242	- **Would the Listings API approve us, and on what terms?** Whether Fringe
243	  approval would be granted to a product that also shows availability badges
244	  scraped from edfringe.com — and whether blending the two sources in one
245	  product is licence-compliant at all — is unresolved and decides the
246	  architecture. One email to Festivals Edinburgh covers this *and* the
247	  static-file question already open on the edinburgh-festival-season page. (New
248	  evidence 2026-09-01, from
249	  [competitor-landscape/](../competitor-landscape/README.md): the
250	  cross-festival planner **planmyfestivals.com** carries exactly the API's
251	  festival set, genre vocabulary, venue-facilities detail and a "Show data ©
252	  the participating festivals" credit, and shows **no availability signal**
253	  anywhere — consistent with an approved, availability-blind Listings API
254	  consumer. Later the same day, stronger: **edfringemap.com states outright**
255	  on [its advertise page](https://edfringemap.com/advertise) that it runs on
256	  "official festivals API data" — while listing every show free, selling
257	  promoted placement on top, and linking tickets out. So one inferred and one
258	  self-declared consumer both look approved, planner/map-shaped and
259	  commercial, which reads well for our chances — and both products' total
260	  silence on availability is what the licence-plus-API shape produces
261	  without a second source.)
262	- **Does Tikketr/equ have any non-public partner API?** Nothing public exists;
263	  a private capability cannot be ruled out. The Society's arts-industry
264	  accreditation channel was also not examined.
265	- **Would any operator actually grant a small site an agent agreement?** No
266	  operator publishes agent terms or rates; only asking answers it. Red61 VIA
267	  agent access terms are likewise unpublished.
268	- **How do venue Red61 instances sync with Tikketr since the platform split?**
269	  Assembly says its box office "syncs live" with the Society's; the mechanism
270	  (and what it means for our availability data's freshness) is undocumented.
271	- **The true size of the PBH unregistered gap.** ~800 own-site listings vs 183
272	  registered shows is page-count arithmetic, not a confirmed count.
273	- **The census's name-matching caveat.** 294 venue codes carry shows vs 301
274	  registered venue records; the 171-venue tail was grouped by hand-checked
275	  substring rules. A registration-data cross-check (operator field, if the
276	  GraphQL exposes one) would firm it up.
277	- **Storm ID's 2027 scope.** Whether the new site replaces the Tikketr
278	  ticketing engine (breaking the scraper) or only the web front-end is not
279	  stated anywhere accessible.
280	
281	## Growth log
282	
283	- **2026-07-31** — page created. Seeded from an 11-agent research pass
284	  (5 web-research topics each adversarially fact-checked, plus a local census
285	  computed from the repo's own scraped catalogue): the Society-vs-venues
286	  architecture and the ≥25% allocation model (explaining
287	  `NO_ALLOCATION_CONTACT_VENUE`); edfest.com identified as the seven big
288	  operators' own storefront via Showcatcher Ltd; the 24-family provider census
289	  with its 171-venue tail and the PBH unregistered-show gap; the verified
290	  absence of any affiliate/agent/API selling route anywhere in the ecosystem;
291	  and the listings-source ranking — official Listings API as the only licensed
292	  catalogue alternative (approval-gated, availability-blind, edfringe-only
293	  linking), Traverse's public Spektrix API and Summerhall's open WP API as the
294	  two genuine venue-feed exceptions, Data Thistle as the only paid aggregator
295	  with real coverage. Two initial research claims were refuted in verification
296	  and corrected here (venue feeds do exist — Traverse/Summerhall; "no public
297	  availability source" is false for Traverse specifically). All claims cited.
298	  Requirements implications (monetisation ceiling, scrape-replacement
299	  architecture) left for human review.
300	- **2026-09-01** — annotated the Listings API approval open question with new
301	  circumstantial evidence from the competitor research: planmyfestivals.com
302	  (profiled on [competitor-landscape/](../competitor-landscape/README.md))
303	  appears to be an approved planner-shaped consumer of the API, and its UI's
304	  total silence on availability matches the API's availability-blind shape.
305	  Question narrowed, not closed — the inference is unconfirmed.
306	- **2026-09-01** *(second pass, same day)* — strengthened the same annotation:
307	  edfringemap.com **self-declares** "official festivals API data" on its
308	  advertise page while selling promoted placement over the free listings — a
309	  second consumer, this time stated rather than inferred, and a commercial
310	  one. The approval question stays open; what changed is that two live
311	  products now suggest the path is passable.
312	- **2026-09-01** — renamed from `fringe-ticketing/` to
313	  `edinburgh-fringe-ticketing/` on the owner's direction: with the wiki's
314	  scope now global (many fringes are in scope), the bare name was ambiguous —
315	  this page is specifically the Edinburgh Fringe's operator census. Content
316	  unchanged; all inbound links updated in the same change.

# Edinburgh Fringe ticketing & providers

Who actually sells an Edinburgh Fringe ticket, who all the venue operators
("providers") are, whether a third party can sell tickets itself, and whether
any provider or aggregator feed could replace scraping edfringe.com. Compiled
once, refined in place.

This page exists to answer a specific owner question — *"are edfringe.com and
edfest.com both just fronts for the event organizers?"* — and the answer turned
out to be half yes: one of the two is exactly that, and it is not the one the
product depends on.

## Key insights

- edfringe.com is an independent charity's box office, not the venues' — the venues' own storefront is edfest.com.
- Every ticketed show must give the Fringe box office at least 25% of its tickets; venues sell the rest themselves.
- One vendor, Red61, powers ten of the fifteen biggest operators' box offices. Provider access is one Red61 question.
- Nobody offers an affiliate or agent scheme — not the Society, not the venues. Deep links earn nothing, anywhere.
- Our own scrape is the provider census: 24 operator families cover 83% of the programme; the tail is 171 small venues.
- The official Listings API bans linking to any ticket seller except edfringe.com — even the venue's own site.
- Only the edfringe GraphQL has availability for the whole programme. The scrape cannot be retired.

## Who actually sells a Fringe ticket

The premise to correct first: **edfringe.com is not a front for the venue
operators.** It is run by the [Edinburgh Festival Fringe Society](https://www.oscr.org.uk/about-charities/search-the-register/charity-details?number=SC002995),
an independent registered Scottish charity (SC002995, income £8.28m FY2024)
governed by an open **£5/year membership** that elects its board — structurally
separate from the operators, and [publicly feuded with](https://www.scotsman.com/whats-on/arts-and-entertainment/edinburgh-festival-fringe-longest-running-venue-operator-says-he-has-lost-confidence-in-the-fringe-society-3791322)
by them at times. The Society performs no curation (open access: anyone with a
show, a willing venue and the registration fee is in the programme) and runs the
central box office.

**The allocation model** is the load-bearing mechanic, from the Society's own
[participant guidance](https://help.registration.edfringe.com/create-or-edit-a-show/payout-and-fringe-allocation.aspx):
every ticketed show must allocate a **minimum 25% of tickets per performance**
to the Fringe Box Office (sliding scale above that), on which the Society takes
**5%+VAT commission**; the venue sells the remainder through its own box office
at its own rate ([Assembly charges 4%+VAT](https://s3.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com/cdn.assemblyfestival.com/Assembly%20Festival%202026%20Information%20Pack%20for%20Performers%20(6).pdf);
[Summerhall 8%](https://www.summerhallarts.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/Summerhall-Arts-Festival-Information-Pack_2025_web.pdf),
and reports that ~70% of its tickets nonetheless sell through the Fringe box
office). This model is why the scrape's `NO_ALLOCATION_CONTACT_VENUE` status
exists: when the Society's allocation for a performance is exhausted, [the
official advice](https://www.edfringe.com/faqs/) is to check with the venue box
office — the ticket may still exist, just not in the channel we can see. In the
2026 data that status marks 1,279 of ~59,900 performances (2.1%), concentrated
at the big operators.

**Platforms:** since March 2025 edfringe.com runs on an interim site built by
Australian agency equ on its Tikketr platform (the GraphQL the scraper hits;
the [official app](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.tikketr.edfringe.prod&hl=en)
is `com.tikketr.edfringe.prod` and takes [~30% of all ticket sales](https://www.edfringe.com/about-us/news-and-blog/our-digital-transformation-strategy-march-2025/)).
[Red61 ran the Society box office 2009–2023](https://www.red61.com/news/red61-celebrates-20-years-at-the-edinburgh-festival-fringe/)
and still powers the venue side (17 federated VIA instances in 2024). A
permanent replacement site is being [built by Storm ID for Fringe 2027](https://www.edfringe.com/about-us/news-and-blog/fringe-society-appoints-storm-id-to-develop-new-website-for-the-fringe/) —
meaning **the scraper's target platform is explicitly interim**.

## edfest.com — the venues' own storefront

The other half of the owner's premise is correct. [edfest.com](https://edfest.com/about)
is operated by **Showcatcher Ltd** ([company 07628569](https://find-and-update.company-information.service.gov.uk/company/07628569/officers),
lead director William Burdett-Coutts — Assembly's founder and artistic
director): a cross-venue storefront formed by the major operators — Assembly,
C ARTS, Gilded Balloon, Just the Tonic, Pleasance, Underbelly, ZOO (Summerhall
was an eighth founder and has left the list). It explicitly
[acts "as an agent on behalf of multiple venues and producers"](https://edfest.com/faqs)
on Red61 rails, sells only participating venues' shows in one basket, caps
booking fees at £5, and fronts the [Love the Fringe membership](https://theqr.co.uk/2026/06/04/edfest-2026-launch-fringe-crisis-how-to-save-on-tickets/).
So the accurate map: **edfringe.com = the charity's central box office;
edfest.com = the big operators' joint venture; venue sites = each operator's
own channel** — three parallel channels selling overlapping inventory.

(Also answered: **Edinburgh Playhouse** is an [ATG receiving house](https://www.atgtickets.com/venues/edinburgh-playhouse/),
not a Fringe operator — but it *is* [registered Fringe venue 59](https://www.edfringe.com/tickets/venues/edinburgh-playhouse)
in 2026, hosting four big ATG-ticketed comedy one-nighters.)

## The provider census

The completeness question has a clean answer: the Fringe is open-access but
**being "in the Fringe" requires paid registration with the Society**, and
venue registration (free) puts every venue in the
[public directory](https://tickets.edfringe.com/venues) — so the registered
catalogue we already scrape **is by construction the exhaustive universe** of
providers. Our `data/venues.json` carries 301 registered venue records for
2026; grouping the 294 venues that carry shows in
[`data/normalized/shows.json`](https://github.com/missingbulb/EdFringeNow/blob/main/data/normalized/shows.json)
by operator family gives the census (computed 2026-07-31, 4,100 shows):

| Operator | Venues | Shows | Own online box office |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| theSpaceUK | 6 | 483 | Red61 (tickets.thespaceuk.com) |
| Laughing Horse Free Festival | 18 | 320 | free; PWYC advance via Fringe box office |
| Assembly | 8 | 300 | Red61 (assemblyfestival.com) |
| Pleasance | 5 | 271 | Red61 (pleasance.co.uk `/via/tickets/…`) |
| Just the Tonic | 7 | 216 | Red61 (edinburgh.justthetonic.com) |
| Hoots | 5 | 201 | — |
| Greenside | 2 | 200 | none found — effectively edfringe-only |
| Gilded Balloon | 4 | 198 | Red61 (tickets.gildedballoon.co.uk) |
| Underbelly | 4 | 193 | Red61 (underbellyedinburgh.co.uk) |
| PBH's Free Fringe | 25 | 190 | unticketed — bucket donations only |
| Monkey Barrel | 5 | 144 | Line-Up for own sales; Fringe runs via edfringe |
| C ARTS / C venues | 4 | 111 | Red61 (CtheArts.com) |
| The Stand | 6 | 109 | in-house (thestand.co.uk) |
| Summerhall | 1 | 82 | Red61 (tickets.summerhallarts.co.uk) |
| Paradise Green | 2 | 75 | volunteer-run non-profit |
| EIFF (Film Festival screenings) | 6 | 63 | own festival ticketing |
| Braw Venues (Hill St, Grand Lodge) | 2 | 58 | — |
| ZOO | 2 | 51 | Red61 (tickets.zoofestival.co.uk) |
| Royal Scots Club | 3 | 34 | — |
| Scottish Storytelling Centre | 1 | 33 | Red61 |
| Scottish Comedy Festival | 2 | 26 | — |
| Traverse | 3 | 12 | **Spektrix — publicly readable API** |
| Bedlam (EUTC) | 1 | 12 | — |
| French Institute | 1 | 3 | — |

The remaining **171 venues carry 715 shows (17%)** — churches, pubs, one-room
independents (largest: Edinburgh New Town Church, 43 shows; The Jazz Bar, 37).
The census caveat: grouping is by venue-name matching, so a mis-named venue can
mis-file — treat counts as ±small, not gospel.

**The one gap in "exhaustive":** [PBH's Free Fringe makes Society registration
optional](https://freefringe.org.uk/performers-faq/) ("It's not compulsory to be
in the program"). PBH's own site lists roughly 800 entries for 2026; only 183
PBH shows are in the edfringe catalogue. Those unregistered shows exist only in
PBH's listings and the printed Wee Blue Book — invisible to edfringe, to the
official Listings API, and to us. [Laughing Horse requires registration](https://freefestival.co.uk/Perform_with_us.aspx)
("All of our shows must be entered into the Official Fringe Programme"), so its
320 shows are fully covered. Free shows otherwise appear in the data like any
other (399 shows `FREE_NON_TICKETED`, 23 `FREE_TICKETED`).

## Can we sell tickets ourselves? No — and nobody can

The verified negative, adversarially checked: **no open affiliate, agent,
reseller, white-label or purchase-API route into Fringe ticketing exists.**

- The **Fringe Society** offers no scheme of any kind; its
  [ticketing T&Cs](https://tickets.edfringe.com/terms-and-conditions) bar using
  tickets "for any commercial, business or re-sale purposes", and its current
  Tikketr platform has no public partner API at all.
- **No venue operator** advertises an affiliate or agent programme. The big
  operators channelled exactly this energy into their own closed joint venture —
  edfest.com — rather than opening a channel to outsiders.
- The **platform layer** has the technology but not the access:
  [Spektrix runs a dedicated Agency API](https://integrate.spektrix.com/docs/agentguide)
  (third-party agents buying on a credit agreement the venue sets up per-agent)
  and [Red61 VIA offers APIs, white-label sales and cross-selling](https://www.red61.com/ticketing-solutions/) —
  but in every case access is granted per-client under a negotiated commercial
  agreement. No self-service signup, no published rates.
- Existing "third-party sellers" prove the pattern: See Tickets and Ents24
  retail [The Stand's own club shows](https://www.seetickets.com/venue/the-stand-comedy-club/8933)
  under explicit venue agency deals; TodayTix and Fever carry **no** actual
  Edinburgh Fringe inventory (London transfers and previews only); LivingSocial
  retails Love the Fringe *memberships*, not tickets. New for 2026, a
  [Sold Out Board lottery pilot](https://www.theticketingbusiness.com/2026/07/west-end-style-lottery-ticketing-system-coming-to-edinburgh-fringe/)
  resells last tickets for sold-out shows at face value — also a closed
  arrangement.

Bottom line for this product: "selling tickets ourselves" would mean separate
negotiated agent agreements with dozens of operators across at least five
ticketing platforms, with no published programme to even apply to. The realistic
ceiling is **deep links to each seller — which earn nothing**, because no
commission scheme exists anywhere in the Fringe ecosystem. (This kills the
hoped-for ticket-affiliate revenue path; `shared/affiliates.js` stays a
travel/accommodation monetisation seam only.)

## Can anything replace the edfringe scrape? Mostly no

- **The official [Edinburgh Festivals Listings API](https://api.edinburghfestivalcity.com/documentation)**
  is the only licensed catalogue alternative: free, official, same registered-show
  universe, per-performance start/end/price, a near-real-time
  `modified_from` sync ("a delay of a few minutes"), 2026 Fringe data loaded,
  and a beta [MCP endpoint](https://api.edinburghfestivalcity.com/documentation/mcp).
  But Fringe access is **approval-gated** (build against a randomised
  `demofringe` dataset, [submit the app for review](https://api.edinburghfestivalcity.com/documentation/fringe_approval)),
  it has **no availability/sold-out field**, and its licence adds a sharp rule:
  [links for Fringe shows must go to edfringe.com only](https://api.edinburghfestivalcity.com/documentation/fringe_approval) —
  "not… any other ticketing site, including the venue's own site". An
  API-approved product could not deep-link to venue box offices.
- **Venue operators:** probed directly, the big operators publish nothing
  machine-readable (Assembly: locked CMS; Gilded Balloon: WordPress with no
  event type; Pleasance/Underbelly/The Stand: server-rendered HTML; Monkey
  Barrel: Wix). Two real exceptions, found and verified by live fetch:
  **Traverse** exposes a fully public
  [Spektrix v3 JSON API](https://system.spektrix.com/traverse/api/v3/events)
  including **live per-performance seat availability** (a fetched 2 Aug 2026
  performance returned `available: 19, capacity: 302`), and **Summerhall Arts**'
  festival site has an open [WordPress REST API with events and performances](https://festival.summerhallarts.co.uk/wp-json/wp/v2/types).
  Together they cover ~94 of 4,100 shows — real, but not a strategy.
- **Aggregators:** [Data Thistle](https://www.datathistle.com/what-we-do/for-listings-suppliers/)
  has genuine full-Fringe coverage but is paid, contact-for-pricing; Skiddle's
  API is beta and non-commercial-only with thin coverage; WeGotTickets,
  Eventbrite and Ents24 carry effectively nothing.

**The verdict:** for the full programme *with availability* — the thing the Now
page's honesty depends on — **the edfringe GraphQL scrape has no replacement.**
The defensible end-state is: official Listings API as the licensed catalogue
backbone *if* its approval and linking rules are acceptable, with a slimmed
edfringe probe kept solely as the availability overlay — or simply keep the
scrape as-is, knowing its platform is interim (Storm ID site lands for 2027, so
the scraper breaks on that timetable regardless).

## Open questions

- **Would the Listings API approve us, and on what terms?** Whether Fringe
  approval would be granted to a product that also shows availability badges
  scraped from edfringe.com — and whether blending the two sources in one
  product is licence-compliant at all — is unresolved and decides the
  architecture. One email to Festivals Edinburgh covers this *and* the
  static-file question already open on the edinburgh-festival-season page. (New
  evidence 2026-09-01, from
  [competitor-landscape/](../competitor-landscape/README.md): the
  cross-festival planner **planmyfestivals.com** carries exactly the API's
  festival set, genre vocabulary, venue-facilities detail and a "Show data ©
  the participating festivals" credit, and shows **no availability signal**
  anywhere — consistent with an approved, availability-blind Listings API
  consumer. Later the same day, stronger: **edfringemap.com states outright**
  on [its advertise page](https://edfringemap.com/advertise) that it runs on
  "official festivals API data" — while listing every show free, selling
  promoted placement on top, and linking tickets out. So one inferred and one
  self-declared consumer both look approved, planner/map-shaped and
  commercial, which reads well for our chances — and both products' total
  silence on availability is what the licence-plus-API shape produces
  without a second source.)
- **Does Tikketr/equ have any non-public partner API?** Nothing public exists;
  a private capability cannot be ruled out. The Society's arts-industry
  accreditation channel was also not examined.
- **Would any operator actually grant a small site an agent agreement?** No
  operator publishes agent terms or rates; only asking answers it. Red61 VIA
  agent access terms are likewise unpublished.
- **How do venue Red61 instances sync with Tikketr since the platform split?**
  Assembly says its box office "syncs live" with the Society's; the mechanism
  (and what it means for our availability data's freshness) is undocumented.
- **The true size of the PBH unregistered gap.** ~800 own-site listings vs 183
  registered shows is page-count arithmetic, not a confirmed count.
- **The census's name-matching caveat.** 294 venue codes carry shows vs 301
  registered venue records; the 171-venue tail was grouped by hand-checked
  substring rules. A registration-data cross-check (operator field, if the
  GraphQL exposes one) would firm it up.
- **Storm ID's 2027 scope.** Whether the new site replaces the Tikketr
  ticketing engine (breaking the scraper) or only the web front-end is not
  stated anywhere accessible.

  operators' own storefront via Showcatcher Ltd; the 24-family provider census
  with its 171-venue tail and the PBH unregistered-show gap; the verified
  absence of any affiliate/agent/API selling route anywhere in the ecosystem;
  and the listings-source ranking — official Listings API as the only licensed
  catalogue alternative (approval-gated, availability-blind, edfringe-only
  linking), Traverse's public Spektrix API and Summerhall's open WP API as the
  two genuine venue-feed exceptions, Data Thistle as the only paid aggregator
  with real coverage. Two initial research claims were refuted in verification
  and corrected here (venue feeds do exist — Traverse/Summerhall; "no public
  availability source" is false for Traverse specifically). All claims cited.
  Requirements implications (monetisation ceiling, scrape-replacement
  architecture) left for human review.
- **2026-09-01** — annotated the Listings API approval open question with new
  circumstantial evidence from the competitor research: planmyfestivals.com
  (profiled on [competitor-landscape/](../competitor-landscape/README.md))

- **2026-09-01** *(second pass, same day)* — strengthened the same annotation:

  products now suggest the path is passable.
- **2026-09-01** — renamed from `fringe-ticketing/` to

1	# Edinburgh market & audience
2	
3	The scale of the Edinburgh Fringe and the audience behaviour EdFringeNow is built
4	for. Two decisions live here, not one: the in-the-moment "what can I make right
5	now" (the home site, *Fringe Discover*) and the weeks-earlier "which shows, which
6	dates" (the planner at `/plan`). Compiled once, refined in place.
7	
8	Scope note (2026-09-01): the product's ambition is no longer Edinburgh-bound —
9	the owner's direction is to grow EdFringeNow into a festival-planning product.
10	This page stays the **Edinburgh** evidence base; the wider comedy-festival
11	market it would expand into is surveyed on
12	[festival-circuits/](../festival-circuits/README.md), and the
13	city-pattern question on
14	[festmaxxing-environments/](../festmaxxing-environments/README.md).
15	
16	## Key insights
17	
18	- 2026 delivered 4,232 shows, 2.81m tickets (+8% YoY), and broke the single-day attendance record set in 2019.
19	- Average ticket is £13, and 1,253 shows are free or pay-what-you-want — nearly a third of the programme.
20	- 37% of people struggle to pick a show. Two thirds buy just one ticket.
21	- 78% come to see something they would not normally — they want surprise, not better filters.
22	- A third of the audience lives in Edinburgh. Two thirds travel in and plan months ahead.
23	- Beds may pick the dates, not shows — over half cannot find an affordable room nearby.
24	- Nobody has data on how people choose in the street. Not us, not anyone.
25	
26	## Scale
27	
28	### 2026 festival (7–31 August 2026, now complete)
29	
30	**Final, from the Fringe Society's [closing release](https://www.edfringe.com/about-us/news-and-blog/edinburgh-festival-fringe-2026-concludes-with-its-80th-anniversary-firmly-in-sight/)
31	(31 August 2026):** **4,232 shows** across **306 venues**, **61,277
32	performances**, artists from **77 countries** — **2,805,395 tickets issued**,
33	an **8% rise on 2025**. The same release records a new single-day record:
34	**over 164,000 tickets issued on Saturday 15 August**, 1% above the previous
35	peak (Saturday 17 August 2019). **1,864 accredited industry from 63
36	countries** and **1,091 accredited media from 30 countries** (702 of them
37	reviewers) attended — a finer, larger breakdown than the opening-day "over
38	1,600 industry and media from 53 countries" estimate below, which this
39	supersedes for headcount and country split.
40	
41	**Opening-day release (7 August 2026)**, kept for the figures the closing
42	release doesn't restate:
43	
44	- **4,206 shows** across **299 venues**, **over 60,000 performances**, artists
45	  from **74 countries**, plus 14 country showcases and four spotlight projects.
46	- **440 free shows** and **813 pay-what-you-want/can shows** — 1,253 together,
47	  close to 30% of the programme. The **average ticket price is £13**.
48	- Genre split at the 4 June launch: **1,401 comedy**, **1,025 theatre**, **168
49	  musicals and opera** (not restated in either release).
50	
51	**The gap between the two releases is itself a finding.** 26 more shows, 7
52	more venues, 3 more countries and roughly 1,277 more performances appear
53	between the 7 August opening-day count and the 31 August close — so a Fringe
54	count is not final on opening day either; it keeps moving through the run.
55	
56	**Correction — the launch snapshot undercounts, and this page had it backwards.**
57	Until this pass the page recorded 3,649 shows / 258 venues / 53,884 performances
58	/ 71 countries and concluded that 2026 was **"smaller than 2025 on both counts
59	(3,893 shows / 301 venues)"**. That conclusion was wrong, because it compared a
60	*programme-launch snapshot* with a *delivered festival*. The Society states that
61	**a further 553 shows registered after the printed programme launched on 4
62	June** — so the June number was ~15% short of the opening-day one, and 2026 in
63	fact finished **larger** than 2025 on both counts (4,232 vs 3,893 shows, 306
64	vs 301 venues, per the 31 August close). The 4 June figures are kept above
65	only as the launch-day genre split; they are not the festival's size. The
66	general lesson for anything that reads
67	these numbers: **a Fringe count is only final once the festival opens**, and
68	registration continues right up to it — and, the 2026-09-11 pass above found,
69	a little further still, into the festival itself.
70	
71	This is still two orders of magnitude more than any one visitor can see.
72	
73	### 2025 festival (still the newest site-traffic and review data)
74	
75	- **3,893 shows** across **301 venues**, **53,942 performances**, artists from
76	  **62 countries**.
77	- **~2.6 million tickets** issued (2,604,404) — roughly flat on 2024, still below
78	  the 2019 pre-pandemic peak of about 3 million. (Superseded as the newest
79	  ticket count 2026-09-11: 2026's own 2,805,395, above.)
80	- **edfringe.com took over 3 million visits and 37 million page views**, and
81	  ~4,300 professional reviews were uploaded to the site to help audiences choose
82	  — no 2026 equivalent found yet, so these two figures are still the newest
83	  on the page.
84	
85	This scale is the product premise: the official programme is a catalogue that
86	rewards planning ahead and overwhelms the person deciding in the moment.
87	
88	### A Fringe-only impact study, commissioned but not yet published
89	
90	Every independent audience study found so far — including the ETAG/Festivals
91	Edinburgh impact studies from 2011 and 2015/16 — measured **all** the Edinburgh
92	festivals together, never the Fringe on its own. That changes in 2026: the
93	University of Glasgow announced an AHRC-funded study, led by Professor Murray
94	Pittock, examining the Fringe's *own* economic and social impact specifically —
95	jobs, businesses, tourism and the longer-term value of careers that start at the
96	festival. Its announcement is also the first source found here to give an
97	attendee headcount distinct from ticket volume: **~750,000 attendees** issuing
98	the 2025 season's 2.6m tickets and supporting an estimated **3,000 jobs**. Both
99	its figures are the 2025 season's — the 2026 totals above supersede them as
100	ticket counts, but no 2026 attendee headcount has been published, so ~750,000
101	remains the only figure of its kind on this page. It is consistent with the
102	[two-thirds-buy-one-ticket finding](#the-overwhelm--decision-problem) below:
103	repeat attendance plausibly accounts for the gap between attendee and ticket
104	counts.
105	
106	### The Fringe is not all of August
107	
108	The page's scale figures — and the product built on them — cover one festival.
109	Seven others run concurrently: the International Festival (147 performances),
110	the Military Tattoo (nightly), the Deaf Festival (80+ events), the Film Festival
111	(38 features), the Art Festival (40+ mostly-free exhibitions), the Book Festival
112	(~600 events) and Fringe by the Sea. Roughly 900 further events, overlapping the
113	Fringe almost completely in time and largely in place.
114	
115	That changes the overwhelm problem's shape rather than only its size. The Fringe
116	is ~80% of August's events, so any relevance- or proximity-ranked list shows a
117	Fringe-only city; and the non-Fringe events are the *scarcer* ones — a Fringe
118	show plays ~25 times, a Book Festival author appears once. The programme's scale
119	buries exactly what cannot be seen twice. Dates, counts, locations, the six
120	different shapes an "event" takes across these festivals, and whether the data is
121	obtainable are all worked through on
122	[edinburgh-festival-season/](../edinburgh-festival-season/README.md).
123	
124	## The overwhelm / decision problem
125	
126	Fringe Society audience data puts numbers on it:
127	
128	- **37% of audiences struggled to pick a show** to go and see.
129	- **Two thirds of ticket buyers bought only one ticket** — for most of the
130	  audience the Fringe is a single decision, not a curated run of shows.
131	- **78% came to the Fringe to see something they wouldn't go and see otherwise** —
132	  the appetite is for discovery, not for a known quantity.
133	
134	The standard advice around that, consistent across guides and relevant to both
135	surfaces:
136	
137	- With more than 3,800 shows, choosing "can feel like a daunting task"; the
138	  advice is to lean on filters, star ratings and reviews, and to **embrace
139	  serendipity** — the show you'd never have booked is often the one people still
140	  talk about.
141	- **Leave travel time.** Edinburgh is compact but August streets are not; guides
142	  repeat that venues which look close together are not close in August — the
143	  reachability constraint Fringe Discover makes first-class rather than an
144	  afterthought.
145	- **Two to three shows a day** is the pace commonly advised as comfortable —
146	  leaving room to eat, walk, and stand still.
147	- **Don't fill the day.** Fringe CEO Tony Lankester's "rule of thirds" — about a
148	  third of the time pre-planned, the rest left open — alongside reporting that
149	  visitors who combined structured planning with open time were more satisfied
150	  than those who over-scheduled.
151	
152	That last point is load-bearing here: the gaps a planner deliberately leaves are
153	exactly the gaps the live surface exists to fill.
154	
155	## Two crowds, not one
156	
157	This page previously described a single audience (the in-the-moment one) because
158	it was seeded from the *Fringe Discover* brief. The repo now ships two front
159	ends — the mobile-first home site and the desktop-first planner at `/plan` — and
160	they serve different people, or the same people in different states.
161	
162	### A. Live, in-festival — "what can I make right now"
163	
164	- **On the ground, deciding for the next hour or two.** Location, travel mode and
165	  the next commitment are the constraints; the catalogue is noise.
166	- **A third of the audience lives in Edinburgh** — locals have no trip to plan and
167	  no accommodation to book, and decide close to the moment by construction.
168	- **Same-day supply is a real channel, and an in-person one.** The Half Price Hut
169	  sells same-day (and next-morning) tickets from the Fringe Box Office only — not
170	  online, not in the app — opening 12 August in 2026, 10:00–18:00 daily.
171	- **Walk-up availability is not constant across the run.** Guides report walk-ups
172	  are easy in the opening week and that by weeks two and three popular shows —
173	  comedy headliners especially — sell out days in advance. The live surface's
174	  usefulness therefore moves with the calendar as well as the hour.
175	- **How the decision is actually made in the street is undocumented.** Posters,
176	  Royal Mile flyering, star ratings and word of mouth clearly drive a large share
177	  of it, but practitioners writing about Fringe marketing state plainly that
178	  nobody knows what works — there is no measured breakdown of in-the-moment
179	  discovery channels to cite.
180	
181	### B. Trip planners optimising around favourite shows
182	
183	- **Two thirds of the audience come from outside Edinburgh** — they choose dates,
184	  book beds and travel, and assemble a show list long before August.
185	- **Audiences now engage months ahead.** Reporting on how the Fringe audience has
186	  changed describes a 2026 audience that follows artists online, votes in polls
187	  and treats the festival as a live-entertainment marketplace well before August —
188	  a marked shift from the "turn up and grab a flyer" Fringe of a decade ago.
189	- **Accommodation binds *which dates* a trip can happen**, not as a footnote:
190	  coverage of the festival's accommodation crisis reports over half of people
191	  hoping to attend could not find an affordable place to stay within a 90-minute
192	  commute. Dates get chosen against beds as much as against shows — something the
193	  planner's "pick my best dates" currently ignores.
194	- **The favourites list is the planner's raw material, and it lives elsewhere.**
195	  Shows are favourited on edfringe.com and saved in the official app's *My
196	  Planner* (which syncs to a personal calendar). Getting that list *out* as a CSV
197	  is served by a third-party Chrome extension ("EdFringe Favourites to CSV",
198	  updated per festival year); no native edfringe.com CSV export is documented.
199	  The planner's front door depends on an export path we do not own.
200	- **The programme launch is the season's starting gun.** The 2026 programme went
201	  live on 4 June 2026, with shows revealed in batches from 11 February — so
202	  planning demand exists for months before any live demand can.
203	
204	### The same person, at different hours
205	
206	These are not necessarily two populations. The rule-of-thirds advice describes one
207	visitor who pre-plans part of a day and leaves the rest open; the planner serves
208	that first third and the live surface the other two. What differs is not identity
209	but **state** — horizon, device, inputs, and what "correct" even means. Those
210	differences are worked through on their own page:
211	[audience-divergence/](../audience-divergence/README.md). Nothing on this page
212	should be read as implying one merged requirement set.
213	
214	## Audience segments (product-brief hypotheses)
215	
216	From the product brief (`docs/product-spec.md`, an internal hypothesis not yet
217	externally validated): visitors mid-festival on foot without a fixed plan; people
218	with a _gap_ between commitments; locals and tourists intimidated by the
219	programme's size. Decisive in the moment rather than researchers, with an
220	emotional target of "delight + relief."
221	
222	Those segments describe crowd **A** only — the brief predates `/plan`, and no
223	equivalent written segmentation exists for the trip-planning crowd. The partial
224	external evidence for crowd B is the block above (two thirds non-resident,
225	months-ahead engagement, accommodation-first date choice); a validated
226	segmentation for either crowd remains an open question.

256	## Open questions
257	
258	- **Sizing the two crowds.** "A third of the audience lives in Edinburgh" is the
259	  only hard split found; there is still no cited figure for spontaneous /
260	  gap-filling versus pre-planned attendance, nor for how many of the two thirds
261	  from outside Edinburgh are day-trippers (no accommodation decision) versus
262	  multi-night stays (the planner's real crowd).
263	- **How the in-the-moment decision is really made.** Still no measured breakdown
264	  of in-street discovery channels — the honest current answer is that nobody has
265	  the data. A small first-party observation (even n=20 on the Royal Mile) would
266	  beat the citation vacuum.
267	- **When planning happens.** No cited series for advance-versus-same-day
268	  purchasing, or for how sales pace across the run. This decides whether the
269	  planner is a June–July product or an all-August one.
270	- **Does the favourites list have a native export?** The third-party CSV
271	  extension exists; whether edfringe.com itself offers an export — and how many
272	  people ever produce one — is unconfirmed, and the planner's intake depends on
273	  it. (Sharpened 2026-08-09: a rival planner, edfringeplanner.co.uk, advertises
274	  that it "takes your favourites from edfringe.com", so *some* route out exists —
275	  whether it is a native export, the same extension, or a login-scrape is
276	  unknown. See [competitor-landscape/](../competitor-landscape/README.md).)
277	- **Do the price figures survive contact with the data?** New this pass: a £13
278	  average ticket and 1,253 free / pay-what-you-want shows are the first cited
279	  price numbers this wiki has. The product brief still says we hold no price
280	  beyond a free/paid flag, and the scraped GraphQL only carries `priceType` —
281	  so this is a published aggregate we cannot currently reproduce or attribute
282	  per show. Whether the official Listings API's `price` field would close that
283	  is on [edinburgh-festival-season/](../edinburgh-festival-season/README.md).
284	- **How much does the programme still move during the run?** Answered in part
285	  2026-09-11: it does — 26 more shows, 7 more venues and 3 more countries
286	  appear between the 7 August opening-day count and the 31 August close. What
287	  remains open is the *shape* of that movement — net registrations, or a mix
288	  of additions and cancellations/pulls — which decides how often the catalogue
289	  must be refreshed to stay honest through the run, not just before it.
290	- **Accommodation as a planning input.** No authoritative price/availability
291	  series found (guide-site figures only). If beds constrain dates more than shows
292	  do, "pick my best dates" optimises the wrong variable — worth evidence before
293	  acting on it.
294	- **Do Fringe-goers attend a second festival?** Narrowed 2026-08-16, not
295	  answered: no *Fringe-specific* crossover figure was found with byte-verified
296	  sourcing (this environment's network egress blocks every source domain that
297	  might carry one). The closest lead is second-hand and imperfect: ETAG's
298	  2011 and 2015/16 Edinburgh Festivals Impact Studies both measured audience
299	  behaviour across **all** the Edinburgh festivals together, never the Fringe
300	  specifically, and only the older one's search-indexed summary mentions a
301	  cross-festival attendance figure at all (~50-70% depending on festival) —
302	  unverifiable and now 15 years stale. The 2026 Pittock study (see Scale,
303	  above) is the one to watch: if it surveys audiences rather than only
304	  desk-modelling economic flows, it may be the first source able to answer
305	  this with current, Fringe-specific data. Still matters for the same reason:
306	  the case for widening the product past the Fringe rests on an unmeasured
307	  assumption that the eight August audiences would go to each other's
308	  festivals if they knew.
309	- **When will the Pittock study publish, and what will it measure?**
310	  Announced 2026 (University of Glasgow, AHRC-funded); no publication date or
311	  methodology detail found. Worth a follow-up pass once it lands.
312	- **Does the record single-day attendance (164,000+ tickets, Sat 15 Aug 2026)
